headline: From clothed scans to 3D joint coordinates.
intro: I turned a lab prototype into a Python research tool that combines pose detections from rendered views and exports estimated 3D joints.
role: Python/VTK adaptation, coordinate-frame debugging, desktop interface, and macOS/Windows packaging.

hero.alt: Illustrated synthetic mannequin with pose landmarks and rays converging from several rendered viewpoints.
hero.caption: An illustrated view of the reconstruction pipeline. All geometry is synthetic.
hero.credit: Original explanatory graphic created for this portfolio.

metrics.label: Candidate landmarks per image
metrics.note: OpenPose BODY_25; low-confidence detections are filtered.

metrics.label: Desktop platforms
metrics.note: Delivered macOS and Windows application packages.

question.title: How do 2D pose detections become 3D joints?
question.text: The lab's method used multiple views of a clothed mesh. My challenge was to reproduce the C# prototype in Python and keep image coordinates, camera transforms, and scan coordinates consistent.

steps.title: Render the scan
steps.text: Load a PLY mesh in VTK and render the configured views, retaining the corresponding camera transforms.

steps.title: Recover spatial rays
steps.text: Run OpenPose, filter detections by confidence, and map accepted points back into the scan's coordinate frame.

steps.title: Estimate and export
steps.text: Combine observations through ray-distance optimization, then visualize joints and export coordinates through a batch desktop interface.

gallery.alt: Diagram of nine rendered images and an early sequence of eight transforms, highlighting the unpaired repeated endpoint.
gallery.caption: A mismatch I diagnosed: nine rendered images, but eight stored transforms. Correcting the correspondence restored alignment.
gallery.credit: Illustration based on the documented development issue; no research output is displayed.

finding.title: Geometry debugging became part of the product.
finding.text: I resolved the image-to-transform mismatch, then delivered selectable batch processing, progress logs, optional visualization, and CSV export in a desktop tool.

details: The original joint-estimation method and C# prototype came from mentor Byoung-Keon (Daniel) Park. My contribution was the Python adaptation and research-tool delivery.
The browser demo is a synthetic reconstruction of the workflow. It illustrates processing stages, not measured anatomical accuracy or the original executable.
credits: Research at the University of Michigan Transportation Research Institute, mentored by Byoung-Keon (Daniel) Park.
Pipeline: Python, VTK, OpenPose, SciPy, and Tkinter.
